en.title: Rights, Freedoms & Responsibilities
en.mnemonic: Remember the FOUR freedoms (conscience/religion, thought/expression, assembly, association) vs. the FOUR Charter rights (Mobility, Aboriginal Peoples', Official Language, Multiculturalism) — freedoms come from the 1215 Magna Carta tradition, rights were added in the 1982 Charter. For responsibilities, use 'JOVHP': Jury duty, Obey the law, Vote, Help others, Protect heritage.

en.question: According to the Charter, multiculturalism is described as:
options: A government policy that requires immigrants to abandon their heritage.
A fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage and identity.
A temporary policy lasting only until 2030.
Restricted to French and English cultures.
en.explanation: Page 12: 'Multiculturalism — A fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity. Canadians celebrate the gift of one another's presence and work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony.'

optionAnnotations.explanation: The opposite of Canadian policy. Discover Canada (p. 12, p. 18) emphasizes that immigrants enrich Canada by contributing their unique heritage.

French and English are the official LANGUAGES (p. 19), but Canadian multiculturalism explicitly embraces all cultural backgrounds beyond those two founding ones.

en.question: Approximately how many years of tradition of ordered liberty do Canadians trace back to the Magna Carta?
en.explanation: Discover Canada describes an 800-year-old tradition of ordered liberty dating back to the 1215 Magna Carta.

source.excerpt: Together, these secure for Canadians an 800-year old tradition of ordered liberty, which dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in 1215 in England.

fr.question: À combien d'années remonte environ la tradition de liberté ordonnée des Canadiens, issue de la Magna Carta ?
fr.explanation: Découvrir le Canada décrit une tradition de liberté ordonnée vieille de 800 ans, remontant à la Magna Carta de 1215.

en.explanation: Canada inherited an unwritten constitution from Great Britain, one of the several sources of Canadian law.
